title: Spacetime Sentinels: a Qiskit game that exposes the competition between spacetime checks and magic in low-overhead quantum error detection
abstract: We present Spacetime Sentinels, a game in which the player protects a noisy circuit with spacetime Pauli checks and is scored on the post-selected fidelity and the fraction of shots that survive, with every number computed in Qiskit. The player spends a budget of ancilla qubits on checks found by the qiskit-paulice add-on, must inject a quota of $T$ gates into the protected circuit, and chooses whether to place them where they commute with every check or to ignore the checks. Each move is evaluated exactly with Qiskit Aer density-matrix simulation against a stabilizer or statevector reference, and the evaluation agrees with 50,000-shot runs of the SamplerV2 primitive. We score moves with a fidelity rate $R=F_{\mathrm{ps}}\kappa^{1/2}$, whose inverse square is the sampling overhead of detection followed by rescaling. Exhaustive evaluation of all 5,412 legal moves under two noise models, together with sweeps over five random payloads, reveals three trade-offs that are not obvious before playing. Checks pay for themselves only above a break-even depth: at depth 6 adding checks lowers $R$, while at depth 18 the best number of checks raises it by a factor of 1.103 and lifts the fidelity from 0.629 to 0.886. $T$ gates add no noise on hardware, yet each check removes spacetime locations where a $T$ gate can be placed safely, from all 90 at depth 18 with no checks to about 14 with four, so the optimal number of checks falls as the magic quota grows. Finally, a check broken by a $T$ gate is worse than no check: with sixteen $T$ gates at depth 18, blind placement lowers the post-selected fidelity to 0.158, and retiring the broken checks lowers it further to 0.102, below the 0.628 of the unprotected circuit. The game runs in the browser and in the terminal, and all code and data are open source.

title: What We Could Lose by Trying to Make Mars Habitable
abstract: The recent push to develop Mars terraforming technologies, increasingly driven by unaccountable private wealth, risks the irreversible destruction of planetary records we have barely begun to read. In this sense, terraforming Mars would be akin to the destruction of the Library of Alexandria. Echoing Carl Sagan's words about the library, in this piece we argue that we should not let such an extensive loss of information happen again. As terraforming Mars would melt and destroy the icy record on Mars, we suggest closing an important gap in the COSPAR planetary protection framework, by expanding regulations on preventing biological contamination to preventing large-scale atmospheric modification and destruction of cryospheric and geologic records.
